Otolaryngology · published research

Tympanic membrane perforation

A 24-guinea-pig randomized experiment reported faster tympanic-membrane closure and improved histological findings after combined 630- and 860-nm laser treatment.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 24-guinea-pig randomized experiment reported faster tympanic-membrane closure and improved histological findings after combined 630- and 860-nm laser treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Tympanic membrane perforation category contains one randomized animal experiment. It evaluates tissue closure in guinea pigs and does not provide clinical evidence in people.

Human and clinical evidence

No human treatment trial or patient case series was identified in the exact category. The available finding is therefore limited to a preclinical model.

Animal evidence

Maleki et al. randomized 24 guinea pigs with tympanic membrane perforations to treatment or control conditions. Combined 630- and 860-nm laser exposure significantly improved healing and histological findings relative to controls (2013). The experiment supports investigation of tissue repair mechanisms but cannot predict closure rates, hearing outcomes, or adverse effects in human ears.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The animal experiment combined visible red and near-infrared wavelengths. The available database record does not support extending its protocol to human use or selecting an optimal schedule. Perforation size, infection status, and measurement timing would need to be standardized in any translational study. Follow-up should also include pure-tone hearing thresholds, otoscopic closure, adverse events, and durability after treatment.

Interpretation

This is an isolated animal result. The database contains no human evidence that PBM closes tympanic membrane perforations.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for tympanic membrane closure in people No human evidence identified
Publications and records1 randomized animal experiment.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Only one randomized animal experiment was identified. Combined red and near-infrared laser treatment improved perforation healing and histology in guinea pigs compared with controls, but no human trial or independent replication was found. A controlled clinical study would be needed to assess closure, hearing, and safety in people.
